title: 2022 Mercedes-Benz EQS Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: Eric Stafford
text:
2022 Mercedes-Benz EQS
Car and Driver
Accolades- A truly awe-inspiring interior, more range than German EV rivals, a showcase of Mercedes's latest technology.
- Less range than Lucid and Tesla models, Hyperscreen is prone to reflections in sunlight, floaty suspension on undulating roads.
- The all-electric EQS sedan combines Mercedes's luxury bona fides with noteworthy EV credentials and dazzling tech.

Overview
The 2022 Mercedes-Benz EQS sedan is the flagship of the brand's electrified future and one of the fanciest EVs ever. We even named it to our 2022 Editors' Choice list. Its curvaceous body effortlessly slips through the air for maximum efficiency, and its palatial cabin boasts luxurious appointments and state-of-the-art features for the all-important wow factor. That's made most obvious by the optional glass-covered Hyperscreen dashboard. The sizable EV sedan is offered with a 329-hp, rear-drive powertrain (EQS450+) or a 516-hp, all-wheel-drive setup (EQS580 4Matic). Both utilize a large 107.8-kWh battery that's rated at up to 350 miles of range. While calling the 2022 EQS an electrifying luxury car is an easy pun, it's also entirely accurate.
What's New for 2022?
The all-new 2022 EQS is the first Mercedes to utilize a platform exclusively designed for EV models. It's also the first fully electric vehicle from the company's EQ subbrand to be offered to the U.S. market. It's expected to be followed by a fleet of new electrified models that include the squat EQA and boxy EQB subcompact crossovers as well as the EQE entry-luxury sedan.

Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The EQS450+ features an electric motor mounted on its rear axle that generates 329 horsepower and 406 pound-feet of torque. The EQS580 4Matic has an electric motor on each axle, which translates to all-wheel drive and a total system output of 516 horsepower and 611 pound-feet of torque. The new EQS450 4Matic slots in between the two aforementioned models and offers all-wheel drive capability and more power output to go with it: The 4MATIC model brings 355 horsepower, up from 329 and—more noteworthy—590 pound-feet of torque, an impressive jump from the rear-drive car's 417. In our testing, the EQS450+ accelerated from zero to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds. The more powerful EQS580 hit 60 mph in just 3.7 seconds in our testing. Every EQS rides on an adaptive air suspension and rolls on rims that range in size between 19 and 21 inches. A Standard rear-axle-steering system can angle the rear wheels up to 4.5 degrees, and there's an optional upgrade that can turn them 10 degrees. This technology is intended to both make the 205.4-inch-long sedan easier to maneuver in tight spots and increase its stability at high speeds. Based on our time behind the wheel, the EQS exhibits a quiet cabin and silken ride quality, but we take issue with the car's disconnected-feeling brake pedal and wish its operation felt more natural. Luckily, activating the car's adjustable regenerative braking system allows the driver to avoid needing to step on the limp brake pedal for the most part, letting the system recapture energy by aggressively slowing the car when the driver lifts off the throttle.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
Both EQS models feature a lithium-ion battery pack with a usable capacity of 107.8 kWh. The EPA rates the EQS450+ at 350 miles of range and the EQS580 at 340 miles. Along with the ability to charge the battery from 10 to 100 percent in approximately 11 hours and 15 minutes using a 240-volt (Level 2) charger, the EQS can supposedly replenish 70 percent of its battery–from 10 to 80 percent–in about 35 minutes using a DC fast charger. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test route, which is part of our extensive testing regimen, we observed an impressive 350 miles of range in the EQS580.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
According to the EPA, the most efficient EQS model is the EQS450+, which earned ratings of 97 MPGe city, 97 MPGe highway, and 97 MPGe combined. Going with the EQS580 drops the city figure to 92 MPGe city but increases the highway estimate to 99 MPGe, for a combined rating of 95 MPGe. For more information about the EQS's efficiency, visit the EPA's website.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
Inside, the EQS is lined with beautiful, high-quality materials and outfitted with countless luxury amenities. The roster of desirable features includes extensive ambient interior lighting, headrest pillows for front and rear passengers, and an Executive Rear Seat package. The latter includes adjustable back seats with massage functions, neck and shoulder heating, and an individual tablet to control the MBUX infotainment system. Still, the most notable option is what Mercedes calls Hyperscreen: a giant wall-to-wall panel of glass that stretches across the instrument panel and encompasses the infotainment system. While this digitized dashboard looks futuristic, the EQS does come standard with a more traditional dashboard. Thanks to a completely flat floor as well as a lengthy 126.4-inch wheelbase, the EQS has a spacious interior. Cargo space is also especially generous, thanks to its large hatchback.
Infotainment and Connectivity
The MBUX infotainment system on the EQS is one of its most prominent interior features, especially the 56-inch-long Hyperscreen. While the standard arrangement is a tablet-like touchscreen that extends from the center console and floats above the dashboard, the optional Hyperscreen acts as one massive display that consists of three distinct screens. These include the 12.3-inch gauge cluster, the 17.7-inch central touchscreen, and the 12.3-inch passenger-side touchscreen. Along with the dazzling array of screens, the EQS features a fingerprint scanner that activates individual driver profiles, the "Hey Mercedes" voice-command system, and augmented-reality navigation in the head-up display. Every model also includes six USB-C ports throughout the cabin and a Burmester audio system.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The 2022 EQS comes packed with standard driver-assistance technology, including adaptive cruise control and self-parking assist. For more information about the EQS's crash test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection
- Standard lane-departure warning and lane-keeping assist
- Standard blind-spot monitoring
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
Mercedes' limited and powertrain warranties are competitive with other German automakers, but its terms aren't particularly noteworthy. There's also no complimentary maintenance, which is something BMW offers.
- Limited warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Electrical components are covered for 10 years or 155,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: 2024 Mercedes-Benz EQS Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: Jonathon Ramsey
text:
2024 Mercedes-Benz EQS
- Luxury and tech in abundance, impressive driving range, mesmerizing Hyperscreen.
- Urban driving dynamics need work, staggering infotainment feature set requires time to learn, more physical knobs and buttons would improve daily-use convenience.
- Mercedes’ flagship electric sedan is stuffed with the brand’s usual sumptuous luxury and goes wild on tech but leaves out everyday usability and an engaging driving experience.

Overview
The primary discussions around gas-powered vehicles often concern aspects of driving—acceleration, cabin noise, or ride quality, for instance. The primary discussions around electric vehicles generally focus on their array of features—how many screens, how many apps, and how connected they can be to the rest of your digital life. The Mercedes-Benz EQS electric luxury sedan is one of the best demonstrations of that difference, a mobile digital living room that is far more interesting to experience than to drive. The instrument panel is 56.0 inches of glass-panel Hyperscreen. The navigation system overlays arrows onto a live video of a route so that drivers know exactly which lane to be in and which turn to take. There are wireless charging pads for front and rear passengers, six USB ports, a fingerprint-recognition system, content-streaming capability for the various in-cabin screens, and much, much more. All of this extensive tech comes on top of the opulence implied by any S-Class sedan, from ventilated front seats to heated rear seats with matching pillows, plus gorgeous cabin materials and superb build quality throughout. Unfortunately, Mercedes skimped on the basics of everyday driving dynamics. The EQS is neither pleasing nor engaging to pilot thanks to syrupy responses, unremarkable handling, and odd brake-pedal feel—an ailment that Mercedes claims it’s addressed with a new brake system for 2024.
What's New for 2024?
Mercedes designed an all-new braking system with new regenerative software for the 2024 EQS, which the company says delivers a more confident brake feel. If that proves true, it eliminates one of the major drawbacks we experienced in our time with last year’s EQS. Several other new features aim to improve efficiency and range. An updated battery chemistry produces increased energy density, resulting in more energy for the same battery size. The all-wheel-drive system adopts Intelligent Disconnect, a feature that disengages the front motor to reduce powertrain drag and improve range. Another range-boosting feature is the standard heat pump, which draws heat off the drivetrain components to heat the cabin. Having a heat pump means the sedan’s main propulsion battery doesn’t need to power the cabin heating system, leaving more energy for the motors. Performance and comfort changes start with more powerful motors. The EQS450+ gets six more horsepower and two more pound-feet of torque, with peak outputs reaching 335 horsepower and 419 pound-feet. The EQS580 4Matic gets 20 more horses and two more pound-feet, its motors maxing out at 536 horsepower and 633 pound-feet. Inside, front occupants now enjoy the impressive wall-to-wall MBUX Hyperscreen as standard on all trims; it was only available on the EQS 580 previously. Newly standard equipment for rear seaters includes heated, power-adjustable seats with extended cushions, an armrest with a wireless charging pad, and rear side-impact airbags.

Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The single motor on the rear axle of the EQS450+ produces 335 horsepower and 419 pound-feet of torque. The EQS450 4Matic adds an electric motor to the front axle for all-wheel drive. Combined horsepower holds at 335 horsepower, but torque climbs to 590 pound-feet. The EQS580 4Matic makes a combined 516 hp and 611 pound-feet torque. In our testing, the EQS450+ accelerated from zero to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds. The more powerful EQS580 hit 60 mph in just 3.7 seconds in our testing. Every EQS rides on an adaptive air suspension and wheels ranging from 19 to 21 inches. Standard rear-axle-steering can angle the rear wheels up to 10 degrees. With the 207.3-inch-long EQS being just three inches shorter than a Chevy Tahoe, rear-wheel steering makes the sedan easier to maneuver in tight spots and increases stability at high speeds. In our testing, we found the luxury sedan delivered the kind of quiet and silken ride that one would expect of an electric Mercedes flagship. It’s not as composed around town, however, thanks to our test car’s disconnected-feeling brake pedal. When we get a 2024 model in for testing we’ll see if the EQS’s all-new braking system addresses our issues.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
All EQS models feature a lithium-ion battery pack with a usable capacity of 108.4 kWh. According to the EPA, the model with the most range is the EQS450+, which is said to offer up to 352 miles of driving per charge; the EQS450 4Matic and EQS580 4Matic are both rated for 345 miles per charge. With 200-kW fast-charging capability, every EQS can replenish its battery from 10 to 80 percent in 31 minutes. Plugged into a 240-volt Level 2 charger, getting from 10 to 100 percent takes 11.5 hours. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test route, which is part of our extensive testing regimen, we observed an impressive 350 miles of range in the EQS580.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
The EPA estimates that the EQS450+ and EQS450 4Matic will return 95 MPGe city and 98 MPGe highway. The EQS580 4Matic is slightly less efficient and earned ratings of 93 MPGe city and 98 MPGe highway. For more information about the EQS's efficiency, visit the EPA's website.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
It’s not like Mercedes would forget how to make an S-Class just because the powertrain is electric instead of gas-powered. The interior furnishings satisfy every expectation and make a plush home for massive amounts of tech. Even the entry-level EQS450+ comes with LED headlights, air suspension, a panoramic roof, augmented video navigation that overlays arrows onto the map to identify lanes and turns, Burmester 3D audio, wireless Android Auto and Apple CarPlay, cabin climate preconditioning, adaptive cruise control, active park assistant, 64-color ambient lighting, and much more. And there’s also the standard 56-inch-wide Hyperscreen, actually three screens that turn the entire instrument panel into a glass-panel display. Thanks to a completely flat floor and a lengthy 126.4-inch wheelbase, the EQS has a spacious interior. Cargo space is also especially generous, thanks to its large hatchback.
Infotainment and Connectivity
The EQS features a fingerprint scanner that activates individual driver profiles, the "Hey Mercedes" voice-command system, and augmented-reality navigation in the head-up display. Every model also includes six USB-C ports throughout the cabin and Burmester audio. Mercedes’ MBUX infotainment software runs on the standard Hyperscreen. The display includes the 12.3-inch digital gauge cluster, the 17.7-inch central touchscreen, and the 12.3-inch passenger-side touchscreen, all fronted by a door-to-door glass topper. Planned over-the-air (OTA) updates for vehicles with the Entertainment Package Plus will add features like the YouTube web app and Dolby Atmos surround sound.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The 2024 EQS comes packed with standard driver-assistance technology, including adaptive cruise control and self-parking assist. For more information about the EQS's crash test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection
- Standard lane-departure warning and lane-keeping assist
- Standard blind-spot monitoring
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
Mercedes' limited and powertrain warranties are competitive with other German automakers, but its terms aren't particularly noteworthy. There's also no complimentary maintenance, which is something BMW offers.
- Limited warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Electrical components are covered for 10 years or 155,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: 2023 Mercedes-Benz EQS Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: Frankie Cruz; Eric Stafford
text:
2023 Mercedes-Benz EQS
- Mesmerizing technology, indulgent comfort, competitive driving range.
- Disappointing driving dynamics, anxiety-producing brake pedal feel, bring back more physical knobs and buttons.
- The luxurious Mercedes-Benz EQS lineup offers posh appointments and a technology show that wows but its infotainment interface is far from user-friendly, and it's uninspiring to drive.

All-Wheel Drive, Rear-Wheel Drive

Overview
If you're after the most technologically advanced luxury sedan, then the Mercedes-Benz EQS should be high on your consideration list. It's the company's attempt at an electric equivalent to an S-class, and it offers the latest and greatest gadgetry—including Benz's giant Hyperscreen touchscreen, driver profiles based on fingerprint scans, and a whopping six USB-C ports. It spoils its riders with voluminous interior space, gorgeous cabin materials, headrest pillows, massage functions, and neck-and-shoulder heating. However, if you want your vehicle to be a car first and a living room second you'll be disappointed. The EQS leaves much to be desired when it comes to the basics of everyday driving dynamics. It's neither pleasing nor engaging to drive. Its responses are syrupy, its handling is unremarkable, and its odd brake pedal feel creates a sense of disquietude. Mercedes-Benz's gasoline-powered S-class sedan is the cruise ship other luxury-car manufacturers measure their products against. Unfortunately, the EQS EV needs a lot more refinement to reach that position in the world of EV luxury sedans.
What's New for 2023?
The Mercedes-Benz EQS sedan lineup sees the introduction of the mid-level EQS450+ 4MATIC model, which pairs the lower powered EQS450+ with the all-wheel drive capability of the more powerful EQS580 4MATIC model. The automaker has also enhanced the Pinnacle trim level with revised rear seat cushions and comfort pillows, and a new Executive Rear Seat Package includes adaptive lighting. Beyond that, 20-inch AMG wheels are now offered on all EQS models. Mercedes has also launched the EQS580 sedan City Edition, sold in Southern California only, with a limit of 150 produced. This uber-rare City Edition comes with an Unagi Model One Voyage electric scooter, a free ChargePoint Home Flex charger, and other bonuses. Mercedes says a portion of the proceeds from those sales with go to a local Safe Kids California coalition.
What's Your Car Worth?
Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The EQS450+ features an electric motor mounted on its rear axle that generates 329 horsepower and 406 pound-feet of torque. The EQS580 4Matic has an electric motor on each axle, which translates to all-wheel drive and a total system output of 516 horsepower and 611 pound-feet of torque. The new EQS450 4Matic slots in between the two aforementioned models and offers all-wheel drive capability and more power output to go with it: The 4MATIC model brings 355 horsepower, up from 329 and—more noteworthy—590 pound-feet of torque, an impressive jump from the rear-drive car's 417. In our testing, the EQS450+ accelerated from zero to 60 mph in 5.4 seconds. The more powerful EQS580 hit 60 mph in just 3.7 seconds in our testing. Every EQS rides on an adaptive air suspension and rolls on rims that range in size between 19 and 21 inches. A Standard rear-axle-steering system can angle the rear wheels up to 4.5 degrees, and there's an optional upgrade that can turn them 10 degrees. This technology is intended to both make the 205.4-inch-long sedan easier to maneuver in tight spots and increase its stability at high speeds. Based on our time behind the wheel, the EQS exhibits a quiet cabin and silken ride quality, but we take issue with the car's disconnected-feeling brake pedal and wish its operation felt more natural. Luckily, activating the car's adjustable regenerative braking system allows the driver to avoid needing to step on the limp brake pedal for the most part, letting the system recapture energy by aggressively slowing the car when the driver lifts off the throttle.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
All EQS models feature a lithium-ion battery pack with a usable capacity of 107.8 kWh. The EPA rates the EQS450+ at 350 miles of range and the EQS580 at 340 miles. Along with the ability to charge the battery from 10 to 100 percent in approximately 11 hours and 15 minutes using a 240-volt (Level 2) charger, the EQS can supposedly replenish 70 percent of its battery–from 10 to 80 percent–in about 35 minutes using a DC fast charger. On our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test route, which is part of our extensive testing regimen, we observed an impressive 350 miles of range in the EQS580.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
According to the EPA, the most efficient EQS model is the EQS450+, which earned ratings of 97 MPGe city, 97 MPGe highway, and 97 MPGe combined. Going with the EQS580 drops the city figure to 92 MPGe city but increases the highway estimate to 99 MPGe, for a combined rating of 95 MPGe. We expect ratings to remain the same for the 2023 model year since no major changes have been made, and the new EQS450 4Matic should land somewhere in between the ratings of the other two models. For more information about the EQS's efficiency, visit the EPA's website.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
Inside, the EQS is lined with beautiful, high-quality materials and outfitted with countless luxury amenities. The roster of desirable features includes extensive ambient interior lighting, headrest pillows for front and rear passengers, and an Executive Rear Seat package. The latter includes adjustable back seats with massage functions, neck and shoulder heating, and an individual tablet to control the MBUX infotainment system. Still, the most notable option is what Mercedes calls Hyperscreen: a giant wall-to-wall panel of glass that stretches across the instrument panel and encompasses the infotainment system. While this digitized dashboard looks futuristic, the EQS does come standard with a more traditional dashboard. Thanks to a completely flat floor and a lengthy 126.4-inch wheelbase, the EQS has a spacious interior. Cargo space is also especially generous, thanks to its large hatchback.
Infotainment and Connectivity
The MBUX infotainment system on the EQS is one of its most prominent interior features, especially the 56-inch-long Hyperscreen. While the standard arrangement is a tablet-like touchscreen that extends from the center console and floats above the dashboard, the optional Hyperscreen acts as one massive display that consists of three distinct screens. These include the 12.3-inch gauge cluster, the 17.7-inch central touchscreen, and the 12.3-inch passenger-side touchscreen. Along with the dazzling array of screens, the EQS features a fingerprint scanner that activates individual driver profiles, the "Hey Mercedes" voice-command system, and augmented-reality navigation in the head-up display. Every model also includes six USB-C ports throughout the cabin and a Burmester audio system.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The 2023 EQS comes packed with standard driver-assistance technology, including adaptive cruise control and self-parking assist. For more information about the EQS's crash test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection
- Standard lane-departure warning and lane-keeping assist
- Standard blind-spot monitoring
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
Mercedes' limited and powertrain warranties are competitive with other German automakers, but its terms aren't particularly noteworthy. There's also no complimentary maintenance, which is something BMW offers.
- Limited warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Electrical components are covered for 10 years or 155,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: 2025 Rivian Commercial Van: What We Know So Far
author: Andrew Wendler
text:
2025 Rivian Commercial Van
For Sale Near You
See all results for new 2025 Rivian Commercial Van for sale near 228211
Overview
Rivian is now offering its Commercial Van (RCV) for sale outside of its former exclusive agreement with Amazon. The RCV is available in two models, the Delivery 500 and the larger Delivery 700. Virtually identical to the Amazon delivery vans already plying the streets as part of its captive fleet, the RCV shares the same friendly, minimalistic styling less the trademark gray, blue, and white corporate branding color scheme. The current RCV comes with a driver's seat and a small flip-down jump seat as the standard setup; numerous shelving and flooring options are available through Rivian's upfitter program to optimize the layout. The front-wheel drive vans offer a claimed 161 and 153 miles of range, respectively, making them ideal for tight urban environments rather than long-distance deliveries. The obvious bogies in this segment are Ford's E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter. The E-Transit offers less range (108-126 miles, depending on model) and less maximum cargo space, but is much less expensive; the eSprinter offers comparable max payload and cargo space and starts at about $10k less. The Ram ProMaster EV hasn't been priced yet. Still, the Rivian Commercial Van has a handy roll-up rear door and an affable vibe all its own that may appeal to creatives and startups looking to cultivate a fresh identity.
What's New for 2025?
Not much, aside from Rivian opening the order book for sales outside of Amazon's captive fleet.
What's Your Car Worth?
Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
Both versions of the Commercial Van are powered by a 320-hp electric motor that drives the front wheels. All-wheel drive is not an option, although we suspect with a second motor mounted on the rear Rivian could offer such a layout in the future. We haven't driven either version yet, but we suspect the electric motor provides adequate acceleration, even when the van is fully loaded with cargo. 
Towing and Payload Capacity
The Delivery 500 provides 487 cubic feet of cargo volume, while the Delivery 700 offers 652 cubic feet. The additional volume comes from the 700's extended 178.0-inch wheelbase and a 278.0-inch overall length. The Delivery 500 has a 157.5-inch wheelbase and a 248.5-inch overall length. Height measures 114.7 inches for the 500 while the 700 is incrementally taller at 114.8 inches. Maximum payload for the Delivery 500 is 2663 pounds and 2258 for the 700.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
Rivian claims the Delivery 500 has range of 161 miles while the longer Delivery 700 has range of 153 miles. Both use a lithium-iron phosphate battery pack. We do know that the vans are currently capable of both J1772 and CCS1 charging at speeds up to 100 kW, but Rivian hasn't stated if the RCV will make the transition to the NACS (North American Charging Standard) as the vans enter the public domain. We'll Update this section with more details as they become available.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPG
The EPA hasn't released fuel economy estimates for the RCV and we're unlikely to see such metrics as commercial vehicles are often excluded from the government's rating system. When we get a chance, we'll take the RCV on our 75-mph highway fuel economy route and update this story with real-world test results.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
The Commercial Van's cockpit was designed with delivery drivers in mind, and Rivian even consulted Amazon workers during development to make sure it met the needs of the user. The seat is designed to reduce fatigue and features heat and ventilation. The steering wheel is heated too, and a vent is integrated into the wall behind the seat to bring warm or cool air from the climate control system directly to where it's needed most. The bulkhead door between the cabin and the cargo area closes automatically when the driver locks the van and even the keyfob has been specially designed for ease of use, with upward-facing buttons that are easy to press when the fob is clipped to a pocket. For times when a second rider needs to come along, there's a flip-down jump seat on the passenger's side; underneath that, Rivian has integrated a built-in first aid kit.
Infotainment and Connectivity
On the dashboard are two large display screens, one serving as a digital gauge cluster and the other as an infotainment touchscreen. The software interface is essentially the same thing you'll find in the Rivian R1T and R1S models. A 360-degree camera system displays images on the central screen to aid in maneuvering in tight, city environments.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
On the Amazon-branded vans, Rivian includes a host of driver assistance features, including lane-keeping assist, automatic high-beam headlamps, and adaptive cruise control. We suspect these features will also be offered on the RCV available to other buyers. For more information about the RCV's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features are likely to include:
- Standard automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection
- Standard lane-departure warning with lane-keeping assist
- Standard adaptive cruise control
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
All Rivian models come with a generous standard warranty which includes bumper-to-bumper coverage for five years or 60,000 miles as well as a battery and drivetrain policy that goes on for eight years or 175,000 miles.
- Limited warranty covers three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers eight years or 100,000 miles
- Battery-component warranty covers eight years or 100,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: 2025 Ram ProMaster EV Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: David Gluckman
text:
2025 Ram ProMaster EV
- Nicer to drive than the gas ProMaster, low load floor makes delivery people happy, enough range for the average workday.
- Not as refined as rivals, can’t haul as much weight as other e-vans, not rated to tow.
- The ProMaster EV’s main draw is its front-drive configuration and low load floor, but it doesn’t put up numbers competitive with rear-drive rivals.

Overview
Ram's full-size ProMaster has always been somewhat of an oddball in the work-van segment, as it's the only front-wheel-driver in a class otherwise full of rear-wheel-drive boxes. While this affords it a low load floor, which carries through to the electric version, it also limits capability. That said, the EV (which stands for electric van) is a little nicer to pilot than its gas-fed sibling, mostly thanks to the smooth-operating and torquey electric powertrain. As it does with the traditional ProMasters, Ram offers plenty of packages for the EV to suit different van use cases and upfits, and there are various options—like heated seats, a white-noise backup alarm, and adaptive cruise control—that delivery drivers and plumbers alike will appreciate. The ProMaster EV's main rivals are the Ford E-Transit and Mercedes eSprinter, both of which have lower starting prices and higher payload capacities.
What's New for 2025?
Ram fills out the ProMaster EV's ranks a bit for 2025, adding three high-roof cargo van models in regular and extended length. They join the super-high-roof delivery version, which features a roll-up rear door.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
Compare the 2025 Ram ProMaster EV to other vehicles you're interested in
Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The ProMaster EV is powered by a front-mounted electric motor that generates 268 horsepower and 302 pound-feet of torque. In our initial test drive, we found its acceleration to be more responsive than that of the gas-powered ProMaster. Its steering is light but somewhat vague. The battery's added heft is noticeable from behind the wheel. Adjustable levels of regenerative braking are available, but the early-build models we drove weren't equipped with this feature. The electric ProMaster does drive better than the gas version, but both are a bit rough around the edges compared with rivals such as the Ford E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter. While the Ford and Mercedes are rear-wheel drive, the Ram is notably the only electric cargo van with front-wheel drive.
0–60-MPH Times
We haven't yet had the chance to test the ProMaster EV at our track, but we'll update this section when we do.
Towing and Payload Capacity
Ram doesn't recommend towing with the ProMaster EV. Payload capacity is limited to 2030 pounds in the Delivery version and 3020 pounds for Cargo models.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
All ProMaster EV models get a large, 97.0-kWh battery pack that's sandwiched under the floorboards. Ram claims it's good enough for a 162-mile driving range and says the van can be juiced via a 150-kW DC fast-charger.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
There are no EPA fuel-economy ratings for the ProMaster EV. Because of its weight, this testing is not required. That said, we plan to take it on our real-world 75-mph highway fuel-economy test when we get a chance, and we'll update this section with results once we have them.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
The ProMaster EV provides the driver with an expansive, wide-angle view of the road. The cabin is more spartan than those in rival vans from Ford and Mercedes-Benz, but the overall design is reasonably attractive. While the interior materials mainly consist of hard, durable plastics, the dashboard incorporates a host of modern technology. For example, a 7.0-inch configurable display in the gauge cluster and a wireless device charger are both available. The electric Ram van's dash also has a large and easily accessible storage tray below the glovebox. A 12-foot cargo length is standard, but an extended 13-foot cargo length is available. Both utilize a 159-inch wheelbase. 
Infotainment and Connectivity
Every ProMaster comes with a user-friendly infotainment system that uses a 10.1-inch touchscreen. It allows for over-the-air updates and offers a subscription-based Wi-Fi hotspot. Two devices can simultaneously connect via Bluetooth, including wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto; the Amazon Alexa voice assistant is also featured. All models come with a wireless smartphone charging pad and a USB-C connection port.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The ProMaster EV offers a host of standard and optional driver-assistance features. It even can be ordered with a digital rearview mirror. For more information about the ProMaster's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard forward-collision warning and automated emergency braking
- Standard blind-spot monitoring and rear cross-traffic alert
- Available adaptive cruise control with stop-and-go technology
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
The ProMaster EV's warranty is in line with those of electric vans from Ford and Mercedes.
- Limited warranty covers three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers six years or 60,000 miles
- Battery components are covered for eight years or 100,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: EV Range: Everything You Need to Know
author: Dave VanderWerp
text:
When it comes to electric vehicles, range is the all-important stat. Whether or not you make it to the next public charging spot, are able to complete your daily commute, or are instead stranded on the side of the road depends on it.
Range is so heavily scrutinized because EVs can travel on average barely half the distance of gas-powered vehicles before they require a "fill-up," and because gas pumps are far more ubiquitous than public fast chargers. Most EV range discussions are centered around the EPA combined range, as that's the one that's published prominently on the window sticker. For the 2025 model year, 256 EVs have EPA ratings (this includes multiple variants of the same vehicle), and the EPA's combined-range figures span from 141 miles for the Fiat 500e to 512 miles for the Lucid Air Grand Touring on 19-inch wheels and tires.
What is EPA Range and How is It Determined?
As with fuel-economy figures for gas-powered vehicles, EV’s range figures are determined by running the vehicle inside a test lab on a dynamometer—think of it like a treadmill for cars—on the EPA’s drive cycles.
For Sale Near You
See all results for used cars for sale near 189554
These tests result in separate city and highway figures, which are weighted 55 percent city and 45 percent highway to arrive at the combined figure that’s shown on an EV’s window sticker. Unlike gas-powered vehicles, whose highway efficiency almost always exceeds the city figure, most EVs have higher city range ratings than highway. Part of electric vehicles' magic in low- and variable-speed scenarios is their ability to recapture energy when decelerating by slowing the vehicle using the electric motor (or motors) rather than the traditional brakes.
Another way EVs are different is that range and efficiency aren't directly related. That's because of charging losses; roughly 85 to 90 percent of the total energy that comes from the wall makes it into the battery pack. That's why there are two terms used: efficiency, which can be expressed in MPGe, includes charging losses, while consumption, the energy use while driving, doesn't include them.
How We Test EV Range at Car and Driver
Our EV range test is done at a steady 75 mph, because highway driving is where range matters most. If you're looking to cover 500 or 1000 miles in a day, it necessarily has to be done at high speeds. There are just not enough hours in the day to do otherwise. Even the shortest-range EV can manage more than seven hours of slogging through city traffic at an average speed of, say, 15 mph. Also, unlike a gas-powered vehicle, an EV's consumption increases dramatically as speeds rise. Of course, as with all cars, aerodynamic drag inflates with the square of speed, but EVs are particularly affected as most do without multiple gears. So, a higher vehicle speed means the electric motor is spinning at a faster and less efficient point.
For Sale Near You
See all results for used cars for sale near 189554
Included below is a subset of the data from our EV range testing and how it compares to the EPA range figure. Unlike with gas-powered cars, which tend to meet or exceed their EPA fuel-economy figure in our 75-mph highway test, EVs on average only achieve roughly 85 percent of their label value. However, some vehicles, typically those from German automakers, have outperformed their EPA label value in our highway test. It seems that those automakers rate their vehicles’ range much more conservatively than some others. For example, Lucid, which makes some of the longest-range EVs, is far more aggressive in its EPA range values. Although the 410 miles we achieved in a Lucid Air Grand Touring is the longest result of all of the EVs we’ve tested, its only 80 percent of its 516-mile EPA range.
You’ll notice that the biggest underperformer is the electric Mercedes-Benz G-wagon, which achieved a mere 67 percent of its EPA range in our test (160 miles to its 239-mile EPA range). But it makes sense that this brick-shaped vehicle would do comparably worse at the higher speed of our test.
If you want to dive deeper into this topic, we co-authored a technical paper for SAE International outlining this difference between internal combustion vehicles and electrics using our test data.
What Factors Affect EV Range?
Two major factors are speed and ambient temperature. Traveling at a steady high rate of speed, as in our 75-mph test, is the worst case for EVs. Aerodynamic drag increases dramatically at higher speeds and when maintaining those speeds there’s no opportunity to recapture energy while slowing.
Cold weather can also affect range dramatically. One of the many reasons for that is that using the heater to warm the cabin—particularly on EVs that have resistive heaters—sucks a lot of juice. In a test with our long-term Model 3 we found that using the heat can increase consumption by as much as 35 percent and kill 60 miles of range, a significant chunk of the Model 3's 310-mile EPA rating.
How to Maximize EV Range
If you’re driving in cold weather, it will help dramatically to pre-condition the vehicle while it’s plugged in before you leave. This will warm both the cabin and the battery using energy from the grid rather than from the battery pack, which will preserve more energy to use for driving. Another simple way to improve range is to simply keep your speed modest.
You should consider our real-world highway range figures the absolute maximum possible in high-speed highway conditions and, as with our zero-to-60-mph times, it will be difficult to achieve them with any regularity. That's because it involves charging the battery all the way to 100 percent, which is not the EV norm. Topping off the last 10–15 percent is when the rate of charging using a Level 3 DC fast charger slows considerably, and it also leads to increased degradation in battery capacity over time. For example, Tesla recommends limiting charging to 90 percent for daily use. Even on long-distance trips, the stops are determined more by the charging infrastructure than anything else, and the most expeditious method is to top up the battery just far enough—to maybe 80 or 90 percent, keeping it in the speedy part of the charge-rate curve—to get to the next charger.
Range is critical; range is complicated. And if you want to drive an EV long distances and you live in a place where it gets cold, plan on a large buffer between the EPA combined rating and what you actually will be able to use.
Dave VanderWerp has spent more than 20 years in the automotive industry, in varied roles from engineering to product consulting, and now leading Car and Driver's vehicle-testing efforts. Dave got his very lucky start at C/D by happening to submit an unsolicited resume at just the right time to land a part-time road warrior job when he was a student at the University of Michigan, where he immediately became enthralled with the world of automotive journalism.

title: 2025 Ford E-Transit Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: David Gluckman
text:
2025 Ford E-Transit
- No trips to the gas station, cavernous cargo hold, less expensive than competitor e-vans.
- Less payload capacity than the gasser, not rated to tow, no people-carrying version.
- The E-Transit has the same good manners as its internal-combustion counterpart, and packs enough driving range for most around-town outings.

159 Miles
2 Seats
Electric
Rear-Wheel Drive
3 Years/36,000 Miles
Overview
Aside from the blue bars in its grille and a lack of exhaust coming out the back, the E-Transit looks nearly identical to its gas-powered Transit kin. The battery-powered van packs a 266-hp electric motor, which stands in for the available V-6 engines that power gas variants. Unlike its internal-combustion-powered stablemate, the E-Transit lacks a short-wheelbase option or all-wheel drive. It’s also unavailable in passenger van guise. With a claimed driving range of up to 159 miles, the E-Transit is well-suited to in-town jobs, and Ford Pro offers a variety of charging and telemetry solutions to help companies manage their fleets. The E-Transit undercuts its competitors on price, too. In some cases, by tens of thousands of dollars. Rivals include the Mercedes-Benz eSprinter and Ram ProMaster EV.
What's New for 2025?
Ford adds a quartet of trade-specific upfit packages that are available on cargo vans direct from the factory. The Electrician Trade package has drawers and bins to organize parts, as well as reels to hang wire. Meanwhile, the HVAC Trade package features bins and shelving and racks and restraints for refrigerant containers. The General Contractor package has a mix of what’s included in the two aforementioned packs, and the Foldable Shelving package aims to meet the needs of delivery companies. There’s also a new option for fleet operators of cargo vans called Smart Acceleration Truncation, which purports to take cargo load into account to prevent jackrabbit starts—too bad for your plumber who will no longer be able to race for pink slips. Ford will also throw in $2000 for commercial customers to cover charging infrastructure costs.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
Compare the 2025 Ford E-Transit to other vehicles you're interested in
Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The E-Transit uses a single electric motor that powers the rear wheels. Rated at 266 horsepower, the motor gives up a few ponies to the standard Transit's 275-hp gas-sipping V-6, but its 317 pound-feet of torque handily tops the gas engine’s 262 lb-ft figure. Furthermore, full torque is on tap right at step-off, whereas the gas V-6 needs to spin its crank to 3750 rpm to make peak torque. Ford claims it revised the E-Transit's suspension system relative to that of the gasoline-powered Transit in a bid to improve the battery-powered van’s handling. When we get a chance to test-drive the E-Transit, we'll report our driving impressions here.
0–60-MPH Times
We haven’t had the chance to strap our test gear to an E-Transit yet. Once we do, we’ll report our findings here.
Towing and Payload Capacity
Although Ford of Europe claims a max towing capacity of 4409 pounds for the overseas E-Transit, Ford’s American arm does not recommend towing with the U.S.-spec E-Transit. Max payload ratings range between 2799 and 3249 pounds, depending on configuration.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
The E-Transit’s 89.0-kWh lithium-ion battery affords up to 159 miles of driving range on a full charge when properly equipped, per Ford. The automaker offers a mobile charger for charging the E-Transit at home. It also sells a more powerful charging station for garage use. Ford claims a 180-kW DC fast-charger adds 67 miles of range in 15 minutes and that Level 2 charging takes as little as six hours to bring the battery from zero to 100 percent.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
Due to their weight, full-size vans are not subject to fuel-economy standards and therefore don’t come with efficiency estimates. When we get the chance to test the E-Transit for ourselves, we'll subject it to our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test and update this story with MPGe and driving-range results.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
Unlike the standard gasoline-powered Transit, which offers numerous interior configurations, the E-Transit packs seats for two, though opting to delete the passenger seat brings that total down to one. Cargo capacity benefits as a result, with the bigger extended-length-body model, which comes only with the high roof, offering more than 487 cubic feet of cargo room. Buyers with less to tote can choose the long body (the shortest available on the E-Transit) with a low, medium, or high roof. The E-Transit's spartan interior reflects its utilitarian agenda. Still, the van’s relatively compliant suspension tune and car-like interior bits make it a better on-road companion than your typical work truck.
Infotainment and Connectivity
All E-Transit vans come with a 12.0-inch infotainment system that runs Ford's Sync 4 operating system. An onboard 4G LTE modem provides a Wi-Fi hotspot, and a complimentary three-year subscription to Ford Pro E-Telematics provides vital vehicle data and tracking features for fleet managers. It also includes a vehicle preconditioning feature that can set the climate and other functions while still connected to the charger, saving vital battery charge and ensuring maximum driving range.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The E-Transit comes standard with Ford's Co-Pilot360 suite of driver-assistance features. Additional available features include speed limiting, navigation with traffic-sign recognition, and blind-spot monitoring. For more information about the E-Transit's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard automated emergency braking
- Standard lane-departure warning with lane-keeping assist
- Available adaptive cruise control
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
Ford's standard warranty package is fairly basic and falls in line with the industry norm. The E-Transit offers an eight-year/100,000-mile warranty on its battery components, but Ford doesn't offer any complimentary scheduled maintenance.
- Limited warranty covers three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers five years or 60,000 miles
- Battery components warranty covers eight years or 100,000 miles
- No complimentary scheduled maintenance

title: The 2028 Mercedes-Benz VLE-Class Takes the EV Minivan Uptown
author: Joe Lorio
text:
- Home
- Mercedes-Benz

2028 Mercedes-Benz VLE-Class EV
- Nimble handling in town, serene interior, 31.3-inch screen and Dolby Atmos provide a cinema-like experience.
- As heavy as a full-size SUV, priced like a luxury SUV, premium versions with power seat limit travel and recline of driver.
- The VLE delivers the room, comfort, and features of a private jet in an urban-friendly, all-electric package.
For Sale Near You

Overview
Mercedes-Benz and minivans are two terms that are virtually never seen together, at least not in the U.S. market, but the new VLE-class changes that. Smaller than the commercial-focused Sprinter, the VLE is designed for passenger transport, with seating for up to eight. It's also an EV (at least to start) and rides on the brand's new van.ea architecture.
Mercedes will offer a choice of single-motor or dual-motor powertrains, and the 115-kWh battery is estimated to offer as much as 340 miles of range. An 800-volt architecture allows recharging at up to 300 kilowatts. Inside, there's a dash-spanning Superscreen and an available 31.3-inch infotainment display that deploys from the ceiling. Several seating configurations will be offered, including one with ultra-luxurious center-row chairs, the better to serve as executive transport.
Expert Tip: If you're leery of a battery-powered minivan, know that Mercedes plans to add a hybrid version at some point after launch.
Where This Vehicle Ranks
#2 in Best Electric VansCompare the 2028 Mercedes-Benz VLE-class EV with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.
What's New for 2028?
The VLE-class EV is an entirely new model for Mercedes-Benz in the U.S. market.
What's Your Car Worth?
Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
- EV Motors: 272-hp single motor, 413-horsepower dual motor
- Drivetrains: Front-wheel drive, all-wheel drive
The VLE300 has a single, 272-hp motor driving the front wheels. The VLE400 gets a dual-motor setup, which provides all-wheel drive and 413 horsepower. An air-spring suspension is optional, as is four-wheel steering for greater maneuverability. When we drove the Europe-market version of the VLE, we found the powertrains to be exceptionally smooth and appreciated the van's surprising agility. Ride quality is cushy, and the cabin remains quiet at speed.
0–60-MPH Times
- C/D Estimate: 6.4–9.4 seconds
In Comparison: The VLE will likely be a bit slower than its closest competitor, the Volkswagen ID.Buzz, which got to 60 mph in between 5.5 seconds and 6.7 seconds in our testing.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
- Estimated EPA EV Range: 320–340 miles
EPA range estimates are not yet available, but we estimate that the VLE300 will offer as much as 340 miles of range. The VLE400's range estimate will likely come in a bit lower, at around 320 miles.
With its 800-volt architecture, the VLE can recharge its 115-kWh battery at up to 300 kW from a sufficiently powerful DC fast-charger or 11kW via an AC charger. The VLE is also capable of bi-directional charging.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
- Estimated EPA Combined Rating: 85–90 MPGe
The EPA has not yet rated the VLE's efficiency, but we think it will achieve a combined rating of around 90 MPGe for the VLE300 and 85 MPGe for the VLE400. MPGe stands for miles per gallon of gas equivalent, an EPA metric that estimates PHEV and EV vehicle fuel efficiency.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
First Row: The VLE will offer three different seating configurations with seating for six, seven, or eight. Up front, two different center console designs are available: a stubby one that allows walk-through to the rear, and a larger one that fills the space between the seats and includes a climate-controlled storage cubby. The materials are far more upscale than you'll find in a Sprinter and include illuminated air vents as part of the ambient lighting system.
Second Row: The second row can be a three-person bench, two individual seats that can face forward or rearward, or two Grand Comfort chairs. The latter includes tray tables that deploy from the side armrest, a wireless device charging pad, a powered leg rest, and a massage function.
Third Row: For the third row, buyers can get a three-seat bench, a three-seat split bench that's power-operated, or two individual seats.
Cargo Capacity: For carrying cargo, the individual third-row seats can be removed; the rearmost bench seat can scoot forward to make more space. Also, the rear seatbacks can be folded, but none of the rear seats fold into the floor.
Infotainment and Connectivity
- Infotainment: 14.0-inch touchscreen, 14.0-inch passenger touchscreen (optional), 31.3-inch rear display (optional)
- Connectivity: Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto
Similar to the Hyperscreen offered in other Mercedes-Benz models, the VLE has an optional dash-spanning Superscreen. It encompasses three displays: 10.3 inches for the driver, a 14.0-inch central unit, and another 14.0-inch display for the front passenger. In the rear, an available 31.3-inch screen folds down from the ceiling. It boasts 8K resolution, split-screen capability, and a built-in camera for video conferencing.

title: 2026 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: Beth Nichols
text:
- Home
- Mercedes-Benz
- Sprinter
2026 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter
- Cavernous cargo hold, available with all-wheel drive and in multiple configurations.
- Base model costs more than rivals, underwhelming power and acceleration.
- There's a Sprinter for every hauling need, but you'll be paying for the badge on the grille.
For Sale Near You

Rear-Wheel Drive, All-Wheel Drive

Overview
Like other full-size vans, the Mercedes-Benz Sprinter comes in several different configurations: You can get it as a cargo, crew, or passenger van, with differing wheelbases (144 or 170 inches), roof heights (standard or high), and seat counts (from two to 15).
Two turbodiesel engines are on offer, and while neither is particularly powerful, they do a fair job motivating this large vehicle, albeit without haste.
Expert Tip: Mercedes also makes an electric version of this full-size van called the eSprinter. Whereas the diesel-powered Sprinter competes against the Ford Transit and Ram ProMaster, the electric one faces off against the E-Transit and ProMaster EV.
Where This Vehicle Ranks
#2 in Best Full-Size VansFord Transit9/10

STARTING AT: $44,595GMC Savana6.5/10
STARTING AT: $44,605Compare the 2026 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.
What's New for 2026?
The Mercedes-Benz Sprinter carries over into 2026 unchanged.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
Compare the 2026 Mercedes-Benz Sprinter to other vehicles you're interested in
Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.
Engine, Transmission, and Performance
- Engines: 170-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter diesel four-cylinder, 211-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter diesel four-cylinder
- Transmission: 9-speed automatic
- Drivetrains: rear-wheel drive, all-wheel drive
Every Sprinter (save for the eSprinter, reviewed separately) relies on diesel fuel. The base engine is a turbocharged 2.0-liter four-cylinder rated for 170 horsepower and 295 pound-feet of torque. The optional high-output engine is good for 211 ponies and 332 pound-feet. Both feed a nine-speed automatic transmission. All-wheel drive is available but only with the high-output engine.
While not as potent as the 310-hp EcoBoost V-6 in the Ford Transit or the 401-hp V-8 in the GMC Savana, the Sprinter's diesels offer adequate (but not exactly urgent) thrust. Though no van boasts razor-sharp handling, the Sprinter's standard load-adaptive stability control and available crosswind-assist systems at least help keep it out of trouble in dicey situations.
What's Your Car Worth?
Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.
0–60-MPH Times
- C/D-Estimated 60-mph Times: 12.0 seconds (211-hp diesel), 13.5 seconds (170-hp diesel)
In Comparison: Though we've yet to strap our test equipment to a recent Sprinter, we can tell you this is not a quick vehicle. We'd guess the base model would need 13.5 seconds to reach 60 mph, while the higher-output model might take 12.0. For reference, the Ford Transit can complete the same sprint in as little as 6.7 seconds.
Towing and Payload Capacity
The Sprinter can tow up to 7500 pounds when equipped with the high-output engine. Models with the 170-hp four-cylinder are good for 5000 pounds, though wheelbase and other specs can affect that cap.
The Sprinter's maximum payload is 6812 pounds. In order to reach that figure, you'll have to equip the cargo van with the heavy-duty 4500 chassis, the standard roof, the 144-inch wheelbase, rear-wheel drive, and the high-output engine. Crew models can carry as much as 3825 pounds, while the passenger van's hauling capacity tops out at 3307 pounds.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPG
The EPA doesn't require automakers to submit fuel-economy data for full-size vans, nor does it publish such information. That said, the last Sprinter we tested—a 2019 model with a discontinued 188-hp turbodiesel V-6 and seven-speed automatic—returned 15 mpg on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy route.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
First Row: Like other full-size vans, the entry-level Sprinter is pretty spartan inside, but the driver's seat is heated, cruise control comes standard, and Benz offers several extra-cost upgrades to improve comfort, convenience, and driver safety.
Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Rows: You won't find rear seats in a Sprinter cargo van, but the crew model gets a three-seat second row. Standard-length (144-inch) passenger vans can comfortably accommodate 12 people across four rows, while the 170-incher passenger van seats 15 across five.
Cargo Capacity: The cargo van offers up to 533 cubic feet of space for whatever you need to haul. Crew vans can swallow a max of 396 cubes, while the passenger van (when fully occupied) tops out at 117 cubic feet. In our testing, we fit 212 carry-on suitcases inside the Sprinter.
Infotainment and Connectivity
- Infotainment: 10.3-inch touchscreen (optional)
- Connectivity: Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto compatibility (optional)
- Audio Systems: 5- or 13-speaker stereo (model dependent)
The Sprinter, while sort of upscale, is not your typical Mercedes. It's built for utility first and foremost, which helps explain the base model's underwhelming tech setup. Mercedes provides an AM/FM radio that plays through five speakers (13 in passenger vans).
Shoppers can option a 10.3-inch touchscreen, though, and that system supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto connections.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The majority of the Sprinter's driver-assistance features are optional, not standard.
- Standard Safety Features: automated emergency braking
- Optional Safety Features: blind-spot monitoring, lane-keeping assist, adaptive cruise control
For information about the Sprinter's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
The Sprinter's limited warranty is typical for the class, but its powertrain coverage is longer than most. Mercedes doesn't include scheduled maintenance.
- Limited Warranty: three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain Warranty: five years or 60,000 miles
- Complimentary Maintenance: none

title: 2026 Rivian Commercial Van: What We Know So Far
author: Beth Nichols
text:
2026 Rivian Commercial Van
For Sale Near You
See all results for new 2026 Rivian Commercial Van for sale near 0
Overview
The Rivian Commercial Van (RCV) should be familiar to anyone with an Amazon Prime account. Those boxy blue behemoths that pause outside your house and annoy your dogs come from EV specialist Rivian, and as of 2025, other fleet-owning businesses can outfit them for their own cargo-transport needs as well.
Two configurations of this front-wheel-drive electric van are available: The Delivery 500 is 248.5 inches long, while the Delivery 700 stretches to 278 inches. (For reference, a Chevrolet Suburban is about 226 inches long.) That makes for a sizable cargo hold, though Rivian limits maximum payload to 2663 pounds, which is below average for an electric cargo van.
The RCV's range is decent (between 153 and 161 miles), and its design is distinctive, from the lens-like headlights and wraparound windshield in front to the roof-lining taillights and roll-up door in the rear. We can see many startups wanting to wrap the RCV's slab-sided body with their logos.
Expert Tip: Ford's E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz's eSprinter are cheaper ways to carry a lot of stuff sans gasoline.
What's New for 2026?
Deliveries of non-Amazon-branded RCVs began in April 2025. The vans are likely to see few if any changes for 2026.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
- EV Motor: 320-hp single motor
- Drivetrain: front-wheel drive
Both versions of the Commercial Van are powered by a 320-hp electric motor that drives the front wheels. All-wheel drive is not an option, although it wouldn't be difficult for Rivian to strap a second motor to the rear axle and make that possible.
We haven't driven either van yet, but given how quickly Amazon drivers move about, we suspect the electric motor provides adequate acceleration, even when the back is fully loaded with cargo.
Towing and Payload Capacity
- Max Payload: 2258-2663 pounds
Though not intended for towing, the Delivery 500 can haul a decent bit of gear, with a payload of 2663 pounds and a cargo capacity of 487 cubic feet. The longer-wheelbase Delivery 700 offers 652 cubic feet of space but a lower payload rating of 2258 pounds.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
- Claimed EV Range: 153-161 miles
Rivian claims the Delivery 500 can go 161 miles on a charge, while the longer Delivery 700 has a maximum range of 153 miles. Both models use a lithium-iron-phosphate battery pack, capable of 100-kW fast-charging, and the vans have both J1772 and CCS ports.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
The EPA doesn't publish fuel-economy numbers for commercial vehicles, and Rivian hasn't released estimates. If we get a chance, we'll take the RCV on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy route and update this story with real-world test results.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
First Row: Like the exterior, the RCV's interior is simple yet modern. Behind the sliding front door is an elevated driver's chair and a chunky plastic dash that supports a flat-bottom steering wheel and two large screens—one for instruments and the other for infotainment. There's also a fold-down jump seat for the occasional passenger. The RV-like wraparound windshield provides good forward visibility, and a standard 360-degree camera system ensures the driver can see what's behind them.
Cargo Capacity: Behind the roll-up rear door is an empty cavity that fleet owners can spec with shelves and various flooring options. The Delivery 500 van offers 487 cubic feet of cargo volume, matching that of the Ford E-Transit and coming in one cube short of the high-roof, long-wheelbase Mercedes-Benz eSprinter’s volume. The Delivery 700 bests all comers with its 652-cubic-foot hold.
Infotainment and Connectivity
- Infotainment: 15.6-inch touchscreen
- Connectivity: Bluetooth
- Audio System: 3-speaker stereo
On the dashboard are two large display screens, one serving as a digital gauge cluster and the other as an infotainment touchscreen. The software interface is essentially the same thing you'll find in the Rivian R1T and R1S models. A 360-degree camera system displays images on the central screen to aid in maneuvering.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
Rivian equips the Commercial Van with a host of driver-assistance features, including lane-keeping assist, automatic high-beam headlamps, blind-spot monitoring, and adaptive cruise control.
- Standard Safety Features: automated emergency braking, lane-keeping assist, adaptive cruise control
For information about the RCV's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
The Commercial Van receives less favorable warranty terms than Rivian’s other vehicles.
- Limited Warranty: three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain Warranty: eight years or 100,000 miles
- Battery-Component Warranty: eight years or 100,000 miles
- Complimentary Maintenance: none
As more information becomes available, we'll update this story with more details about:
- 0–60-MPH Times
- C/D Test Results and Specs

title: 2026 Ram ProMaster EV Review, Pricing, and Specs
author: Austin Parsons
text:
2026 Ram ProMaster EV
- Better road manners than the gas-powered ProMaster, low floor makes loading easy, competitive range.
- Can't tow, undercut by the superior Ford E-Transit on price, both of its main rivals offer better payload and cargo capacity.
- The Ram ProMaster's easy-load floor and array of customization options are unique appeals, but they are overridden by its high price and lackluster payload capacity.
For Sale Near You
See all results for new 2026 Ram ProMaster EV for sale near 0
Overview
No one is likely to stop and stare at a Ram ProMaster EV unless they're eagerly anticipating the arrival of a recent online purchase. Despite blending into the background, it is a cargo-hauling workhorse, getting everything where it needs to go in silence. The ProMaster EV is one of a handful of electric cargo vans currently on sale to the public, and it has a couple of tricks up its sleeve to stand out from its few rivals. The ProMaster EV is the only front-wheel-drive model in its segment, allowing for a lower floor that makes cargo loading easier. It's also extremely customizable, with several different configurations and plenty of options to choose from. Those are all nifty traits, but the ProMaster EV falls behind its primary competitors in cargo space and payload capacity—critical metrics for a vehicle like this. 
 
Expert Tip: The Ford E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter are the ProMaster EV's main rivals. Both have more cargo space and higher payload capacities, and the Ford undercuts the Ram by a few thousand dollars.
What's New for 2026?
The ProMaster EV is expected to roll silently into 2026 without any notable changes.
If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.
Pricing and Which One to Buy
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
- EV Motor: 268-hp single motor
- Drivetrain: front-wheel drive
The ProMaster EV is powered by a front-mounted electric motor that generates 268 horsepower and 302 pound-feet of torque. In our initial test drive, we found its acceleration to be more responsive than that of the gas-powered ProMaster. Its steering is light and somewhat vague. The battery's added heft is noticeable from behind the wheel. Adjustable levels of regenerative braking are available, but the early-build models we drove weren't equipped with this feature.
The electric ProMaster does drive better than the gas version, but both are a bit rough around the edges compared with rivals such as the Ford E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter. While the Ford and Mercedes are rear-wheel drive, the Ram is notably the only electric cargo van with front-wheel drive.
0–60-MPH Times
We haven't yet had the chance to test the ProMaster EV at our track, but we'll update this section when we do.
Towing and Payload Capacity
- Max Payload: 2030 pounds (Delivery), 3020 pounds (Cargo)
Ram doesn't recommend towing with the ProMaster EV. Payload capacity is limited to 2030 pounds in the Delivery version and 3020 pounds for Cargo models.
In Comparison: The Ram ProMaster EV falls behind both of its primary competitors in payload capacity. The Mercedes-Benz eSprinter can haul up to 3516 pounds, while the Ford E-Transit maxes out at 3249 pounds.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
- Claimed EV Range: 162 miles
All ProMaster EV models get a large, 97.0-kWh battery pack that's sandwiched under the floorboards. Ram claims it's good enough for a 162-mile driving range, which places it between the E-Transit and Sprinter in terms of distance traveled on a charge. When it runs out of juice, Ram claims that the van can be juiced via a 150-kW DC fast-charger.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
There are no EPA fuel-economy ratings for the ProMaster EV. Because of its weight, this testing is not required. That said, we plan to take it on our real-world 75-mph highway fuel-economy test when we get a chance, and we'll update this section with results once we have them.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
First Row: The ProMaster EV provides the driver with an expansive, wide-angle view of the road. The cabin is more spartan than those in rival vans from Ford and Mercedes-Benz, but the overall design is reasonably attractive. While the interior materials mainly consist of hard, durable plastics, the dashboard incorporates a host of modern technology. For example, a 7.0-inch configurable display in the gauge cluster and a wireless device charger are both available.
Cargo Capacity: A 12-foot cargo length is standard, but an extended 13-foot cargo length is available. Both utilize a 159-inch wheelbase. The ProMaster EV offers up to 463 cubic feet of interior cargo volume, which is less than the max volume of both the Ford E-Transit and Mercedes-Benz eSprinter.
Infotainment and Connectivity
- Infotainment: 10.1-inch touchscreen
- Connectivity: Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto
- Audio System: four-speaker audio system (Standard)
Every ProMaster comes with a user-friendly infotainment system that uses a 10.1-inch touchscreen. It allows for over-the-air updates and offers a subscription-based Wi-Fi hotspot. Two devices can simultaneously connect via Bluetooth, including wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto; the Amazon Alexa voice assistant is also featured. All models come with a wireless smartphone charging pad and a USB-C connection port.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
The ProMaster EV offers a host of standard and optional driver-assistance features. It can even be ordered with a digital rearview mirror.
- Standard Safety Features: forward-collision warning and automated emergency braking, blind-spot monitoring and rear cross-traffic alert
- Optional Safety Features: adaptive cruise control with stop-and-go technology
For information about the ProMaster EV's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
The ProMaster EV's warranty is in line with those of electric vans from Ford and Mercedes.
- Limited Warranty: three years or 36,000 miles
- Powertrain Warranty: six years or 60,000 miles
- Complimentary Maintenance: none

author: Eric Stafford
text:
- Home
- Volkswagen
- ID.Buzz
2025 Volkswagen ID.Buzz Microbus
Car and Driver
Accolades- Charming and nostalgic design both inside and out, huge amount of space inside, AWD model offers strong acceleration.
- Real-world highway range falls short, inconsistent brake-pedal feel, interface is overly reliant on touch-sensitive controls.
- The ID.Buzz serves up a healthy portion of nostalgic charm, acting as VW's halo model while also providing EV shoppers with a practical choice for families.

Overview
With electric vehicles becoming more mainstream each year, and few capacious EV options for families, the 2025 Volkswagen ID.Buzz addresses a largely untapped market. The design of the ID.Buzz commemorates the German company's iconic Type 2 Microbus—or VW Bus for short—which inspired the new van's retro design. Along with its uniquely nostalgic exterior aesthetic, its spacious cabin features flexible seating and three rows. The ID.Buzz's all-electric powertrain comes in rear- and all-wheel-drive configurations, delivering a driving range of up to 234 miles. Plugged into a DC fast-charger, VW says the van will be able to charge its battery from 10 to 80 percent in 30 minutes. The ID.Buzz can be considered a competitor to conventional minivans such as the Honda Odyssey and the Toyota Sienna, but its distinctive styling, spacious interior, and electric powertrain make it both a standout in its segment and a member of our 10Best Trucks list for 2025. As one of our favorites in its segment, the Volkswagen ID.Buzz has also earned a spot on our Editors' Choice list for 2025.
What's New for 2025?
The ID.Buzz's arrival in the U.S. has been a long time coming, and it marks the Volkswagen van's highly anticipated return to our shores.
What's Your Car Worth?

Pricing and Which One to Buy
Compare the 2025 Volkswagen ID.Buzz to other vehicles you're interested in
Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.
EV Motor, Power, and Performance
The ID.Buzz uses Volkswagen's Modular Electric Drive (MEB) platform that also underpins the Audi Q4 e-tron crossover and the VW ID.4 crossover. While Europe gets both a commercial and passenger version of the ID.Buzz, in America the long-wheelbase passenger van is the only model available. The base model features a single, rear-mounted electric motor that makes 282 horsepower. A dual-motor, all-wheel-drive configuration with 335 horsepower is also offered. In our test drive of the all-wheel-drive ID.Buzz, we found that it offers spirited acceleration and a comfortable ride. The rear-wheel-drive version is a bit slower but otherwise drives similarly. It's quiet at lower speeds but can get a bit noisy on the highway. We weren't fans of the brake pedal's inconsistent feel, and the ID.Buzz is quite heavy; fortunately, the placement of the battery pack under the floor means that handling still feels secure.
0-60–MPH Times
In our testing, the all-wheel-drive ID.Buzz got to 60 mph in 5.5 seconds and the rear-wheel-drive model did the 60-mph sprint in 6.7 seconds.
Range, Charging, and Battery Life
The ID.Buzz comes with an 86.0-kWh battery pack as standard, and Volkswagen says rear-wheel-drive models will offer up to 234 miles of range per charge. All-wheel drive models are said to offer up to 231 miles per charge. In our real-world 75-mph highway range testing, we fell short of those estimates, with the AWD ID.Buzz achieving a result of 190 miles and the RWD ID.Buzz achieving 180 miles. VW also claims that those who plug into a DC fast-charger will be able to charge from 10 to 80 percent in as little as 30 minutes; in our testing, the RWD ID.Buzz charged from 10 percent to 90 percent in 33 minutes.
Fuel Economy and Real-World MPGe
The EPA rates the rear-wheel-drive ID.Buzz at 90 MPGe city, 75 MPGe highway, and 83 MPGe combined. The all-wheel-drive model is rated lower, at 87 MPGe city, 74 MPGe highway, and 80 MPGe combined. When we get a chance, we'll take the ID.Buzz on our 75-mph highway fuel economy route and update this story with test results. For more information about the ID.Buzz's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.
Interior, Comfort, and Cargo
One of the defining details of the ID.Buzz is its cavernous and configurable interior. The front seats feature adjustable armrests as well as tables that fold out of the backrests for rear-seat passengers. There's also a removable center console between the front seats. The U.S. version features three rows of seats with space for seven riders; a pair of second-row captain's chairs are available but drop capacity to six passengers. The ID.Buzz's standout standard features include a 10.0-inch digital gauge cluster, customizable ambient lighting, and a set of massaging front seats.
Infotainment and Connectivity
The VW van's infotainment system primarily operates through a 12.9-inch touchscreen that sprouts from the middle of the dashboard. A 10.0-inch digital gauge display is also standard. We also expect the ID.Buzz to have standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and possibly some sort of rear-seat entertainment system. A subscription-based Wi-Fi hotspot and wireless device charging are available, too.
Safety and Driver-Assistance Features
Overall Safety Rating (NHTSA)
The ID.Buzz is offered with a diverse selection of standard and optional driver-assistance technology. Volkswagen also offers a memory function for the self-park assist that is said to work on pre-saved routes. For more information about the ID.Buzz's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites. Key safety features include:
- Standard forward-collision warning and automated emergency braking
- Standard lane-departure warning and lane-keeping assist
- Standard adaptive cruise control
Warranty and Maintenance Coverage
Volkswagen currently offers an above-average limited warranty and below-average powertrain coverage compared with rival non-luxury brands, but it offers two years or 20,000 miles of complimentary scheduled maintenance. The ID.Buzz's electric components are covered for eight years or 100,000 miles.
- Limited warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Powertrain warranty covers four years or 50,000 miles
- Battery components are covered for eight years or 100,000 miles
- Complimentary maintenance is covered for two years or 20,000 miles
